stories.headline: Fast, but never instant: what the speed of light really means
stories.summary: Light in a vacuum moves at exactly 299,792,458 metres per second, a value fixed by definition when the metre was redefined in 1983. Even at that speed, moonlight is about 1.3 seconds old when it reaches us, and sunlight about 8.3 minutes old.

stories.headline: Counting the bones of the adult skeleton
stories.summary: A newborn has around 270 bones. Many fuse together during growth, so an adult is left with around 206: 80 in the axial skeleton of skull, spine and ribcage, and 126 in the limbs and girdles.

stories.headline: The laboratory beneath the Franco-Swiss border
stories.summary: CERN, established in 1954 in Meyrin, a western suburb of Geneva, runs the Large Hadron Collider in a 27 km tunnel about 100 metres underground. The World Wide Web was invented there by Tim Berners-Lee in 1989.

payload.dispatch: Light travels through a vacuum at exactly 299,792,458 metres per second, a figure fixed by definition since 1983, when the metre was redefined in terms of it. At that speed, light from the Moon reaches Earth in about 13 seconds, and light from the Sun takes about 8.3 minutes to arrive.

evidence.title: Two distances
evidence.text: The Moon's average distance from Earth is 384,399 km. The Sun lies one astronomical unit away: 149,597,870.7 km.

evidence.title: Fixed by definition
evidence.text: In 1983 the metre was defined as the length of the path travelled by light in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.

reveal.explanation: Divide the Moon's distance by the speed of light: 384,399 km at 299,792 km per second is about 1.3 seconds, not 13. The same sum for the Sun gives roughly 499 seconds, or 8.3 minutes.

sources.excerpt: The speed of light is exactly equal to 299,792,458 metres per second. Light takes about 1.3 s from the Moon to Earth and about 8.3 min from the Sun to Earth. In 1983 the metre was defined as the length of the path travelled by light in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.
A lunar distance, 384,399 km (238,854 mi), is the Moon's average distance to Earth. The average lunar distance is approximately 385,000 km, or 1.3 light-seconds.
1 astronomical unit = 149,597,870.700 kilometres (exactly), roughly the average Earth–Sun distance.

payload.question: How many bones are in the adult human skeleton?
payload.comparison: A newborn's skeleton has around 270 bones; many of them fuse together during growth.

reveal.context: The adult skeleton has around 206 bones: 80 in the axial skeleton of skull, spine and ribcage, and 126 in the appendicular skeleton of the limbs and their girdles. A newborn has around 270, many of which fuse by adulthood.

sources.excerpt: It is composed of around 270 bones at birth; this total decreases to around 206 bones by adulthood after some bones fuse together. The axial skeleton (80 bones) is formed by the vertebral column, the rib cage and the skull; the appendicular skeleton (126 bones) is formed by the pectoral girdles, the upper limbs, the pelvic girdle and the lower limbs.

clues: The world's largest particle accelerator runs through a 27 km circular tunnel about 100 metres underground, on the border between two countries.
The laboratory was established in 1954 in a western suburb of a city on the France–Switzerland border, and the World Wide Web was invented there in 1989.

reveal.explanation: CERN is based in Meyrin, a western suburb of Geneva, on the France–Switzerland border. Established in 1954, it runs the Large Hadron Collider in a 27 km tunnel about 100 metres underground; the World Wide Web was invented there by Tim Berners-Lee in 1989.

sources.excerpt: CERN, established in 1954, is based in Meyrin, a western suburb of Geneva, on the France–Switzerland border (46.2330°N 6.0556°E). The LHC uses the 27 km circumference circular tunnel, located 100 metres underground. In 1989, the World Wide Web was invented at CERN by Tim Berners-Lee.
